transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-12
Start: 09:17 EDT
Duration: 63 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood PM) / Rajiv (Orion Head ML), Becky (Infra), Tom (Security)
---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we know you had questions on JSON-mode overhead and constrained decoding — quick intro then I'll hand to Ethan for the deep dive.
[00:18] Rajiv: Yep, thanks. We're mostly concerned about two things: first, our latency SLOs at p99 for interactive assistant are 350ms for 1-2k token sessions and second, when we switch to structured JSON outputs it's spiking more than expected.
[00:35] Ethan: Cool. So agenda for today's deep dive — we'll go over what "JSON-mode" and constrained decode do at runtime, where extra token churn comes from, how KV cache interacts with repeated prefixes, and then quant/ batching tradeoffs, plus VPC/on-prem notes.
[00:52] Becky: One quick infra note — our on-prem infra is 8x A100 equivalent; we have standard KMS via Hashi, and strict egress rules.
[01:05] Ethan: Great, that helps. Alright diving in — constrained decoding, quick definition: it's basically constraining the sampling space via token-level masks or grammar constraints to keep the model emitting only valid JSON tokens or invoking tools. That constraint is typically implemented either as a lexicon mask in softmax computation or via a higher-level step that filters candidate tokens. Both add compute.
[01:34] Tom: When you say "adds compute" is that large? Our worry is p99 tail.
[01:40] Ethan: Short answer: it depends. Constraining during decoding can increase per-step work if you re-evaluate logits and apply masks in a way that disables kernel fusion. On some runtimes that means you can't use fused softmax+logits-kernel and you end up with an extra kernel call per token or additional memory copies, which hurts latency especially at small batch sizes.
[02:05] Rajiv: So is that what we're seeing in our tests — JSON forced mode shows +30-60ms per token compared to unconstrained?
[02:12] Ethan: That delta is plausible. Two things to check: are you using a token-by-token constraint (tight grammar) or a chunked validation approach?
[02:22] Becky: We're doing token-level validation currently — generator checks after each token to ensure valid JSON bracket/quote state machine.
[02:30] Ethan: That's the worst case for overhead. Alternative: constrained decode via post-hoc repair or tolerance windows — fewer masks, less kernel interference, but higher risk of invalid JSON needing string parse+repair. There's also hybrid: only apply hard masks for structural tokens (brackets, commas, quotes) and allow freer text for values.
[02:53] Priya: From product side, we care about deterministic valid output for downstream parsers — so repair isn't great.
[03:00] Ethan: Understood. For deterministic needs, we optimize kernel paths: Redwood's runtime supports an incremental masked-softmax path that keeps fused ops but needs specific quantization layout and careful token remapping. On some older kernels, we fallback to unfused path so you get the latency penalty.
[03:24] Rajiv: OK that maps. What about KV cache? We have long sessions with repeated system prompt prefixes and a lot of reuse. We're seeing memory thrash and occasional p99 spikes after ~40k tokens.
[03:37] Ethan: Two things there — eviction policy and prefix/key sharding. If your sessions accumulate very long prefixes without checkpointing, the KV cache grows and can cause GPU memory pressure that triggers slower allocation paths or micro-copy to host memory. Our recommended pattern: prefix compaction and explicit shorter priming windows; also, Redwood supports checkpointed KV snapshots so you can flush older history and rehydrate only recent context.
[04:05] Becky: Is there an automated compaction we can enable?
[04:09] Ethan: Yes — the platform has an adaptive prefix-cacher that detects repeating prefixes and stores compressed KV entries; we can enable it in Dedicated and Private with a config flag. On-prem you might need slightly different memory tuning (CUDA allocator tweaks).
[04:25] Tom: In on-prem scenario how does this interact with KMS? We need envelope encryption.
[04:31] Ethan: We integrate with customer KMS via a local sidecar that handles key unwrap. The runtime never holds plaintext keys in persistent storage; the accelerator memory uses ephemeral keys. For Private/VPC we can enable HSM-backed CMKs — that's supported but requires networking for attestation.
[04:47] Rajiv: Back to batching — our traffic is mostly single-user interactive. What are safe batch sizes without blowing latency?
[04:56] Ethan: For interactive single-user, batch size of 1 is common. But Redwood's continuous batching can opportunistically join similar short-latency requests within a 5-10ms window to achieve amortization. The tradeoff is jitter. If your p99 SLO is tight, keep batching window <= 5ms and limit max batch to 4. For throughput loads we recommend larger windows.
[05:20] Rajiv: Do continuous batches interact poorly with constrained decoding?
[05:25] Ethan: They can. If members of a batch have different constraint masks, the runtime needs per-example masks which increases memory and compute. We sometimes do mask grouping — group examples by mask type before batching — that reduces overhead. But grouping adds scheduling complexity and can increase latency if group sizes are small.
[05:47] Becky: In our tests mask-per-example increased p50 little but p99 got worse, yes.
[05:54] Ethan: Another levers: you can pre-compile frequently-used masks into bitmasks that the kernel supports natively, so mask application is cheaper. This requires model-specific kernel support; Redwood can do that for curated models.
[06:10] Rajiv: Quantization — we tried INT8 and saw generator hallucination rate increase slightly for structured keys (like key names sometimes shortened). Thoughts?
[06:20] Ethan: Quantization changes logits distribution; structural tokens that are lower-probability may get nudged down. For JSON mode that's dangerous. The mitigation: per-layer calibration with task-specific prompts and high-fidelity quantization (QLoRA-style or per-channel symmetric quantization) and fallback logic for structure tokens — keep first/last layers fp16 or use mixed precision. Also run evals focused on structural token recall.
[06:46] Priya: So a tuned quant profile and maybe keep critical layers at higher precision. Cost tradeoff?
[06:53] Ethan: Exactly. Mixed-precision keeps most throughput benefit while protecting structure. On some hardware INT4 gives huge cost gains but you need more calibration and may only be appropriate for embeddings/semantic tasks, not strict JSON outputs.
[07:10] Tom: Any advice for our deployment — Dedicated vs Private on-prem? We need strict audit logs and no egress.
[07:18] Ethan: If you need zero-egress and full control, Private on-prem is the right route. Redwood Private supports a control plane that can be air-gapped; we ship offline artifacts and an operator bundle. For audit logs we forward to your SIEM via local collector. The one tradeoff is slower ops turnaround vs Hosted, but you get deterministic networking.
[07:38] Becky: Does enabling the adaptive prefix cache require outbound telemetry?
[07:42] Ethan: No, adaptive prefix caching can be enabled fully locally; we only ask for optional anonymous metrics for tuning but that's not required.
[07:50] Rajiv: Can you summarize expected delta numbers — like constrained decode overhead, p99 impact, quant gains? Even ballparks help.
[07:58] Ethan: Sure — ballpark and very workload-dependent: constrained token masking worst-case +20-80% per-token latency depending on kernel fusion (so could be +10-60ms/tok on small models, +30-120ms/tok on large autoregressive), p99 impact often bigger than p50 because of extra kernels and memory churn. Adaptive batching with 5ms window can reduce cost by ~10-25% without harming p99 if masks are grouped. INT8 quant might reduce token compute cost by ~30-50% but requires calibration, mixed-precision tradeoffs reduce hallucination. Those are rough.
[08:40] Becky: That matches our numbers-ish.
[08:44] Ethan: Practical plan for Orion: 1) run a focused bench with your 10 prompts across seq lengths and JSON constraints — measure p50/p95/p99 and token-cost, 2) try hybrid mask strategy with precompiled masks, 3) run INT8 mixed-precision profile with structural token evals, 4) if on-prem, enable adaptive prefix cache and tune CUDA allocator.
[09:10] Maya: We'll also send SOC2 + network diagrams and the Private deployment checklist.
[09:14] Rajiv: Great. A few off-script Qs — how does function calling interplay with constrained JSON? We call functions from JSON payloads.
[09:22] Ethan: Function calling is basically structured output where the model emits a function name and JSON args. The runtime sees it as JSON-mode with additional token-level constraints. The overhead is similar; if function calling is frequent, consider a specialized tool where the model outputs just an identifier and small arg list and we do arg assembly off-model. Also caching of previously called function results can avoid recompute for idempotent calls.
[09:44] Tom: For traceability we need per-call request/response audit with hash — supported?
[09:50] Maya: Yes we can attach request IDs and hashed outputs to logs; Redwood Console supports token-level cost breakdown and request hashes for auditing. We'll include configuration notes.
[09:59] Rajiv: Any gotchas with JSON parsing library differences? We've had slight differences between Python stdlib and our Golang parser on trailing commas.
[10:07] Ethan: Good point — realtime: we tend to emit strictly RFC JSON (no trailing commas). But when using repair heuristics watch for differences; better to define a strict schema and use schema-based constrained generation which enforces tokens exactly.
[10:22] Becky: Ok last — timeline. If we run bench next week what's realistic?
[10:27] Maya: Ethan can start tests once you provide prompts; we'll package results and propose POC kickoff the following week.
[10:33] Rajiv: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[10:36] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up with notes and links.
